source_read: PMC HTML (saved text of PMC3764482, NIH author manuscript), read start to end: opening commentary, keywords, history and epidemiology, Pharmacology and Toxicology, Neuropsychiatric Complications, Formication, Stereotypy or Punding, Parkinson's disease, Choreoathetoid Movements and Dyskinesias, Dental Caries, Summary, Key Points, acknowledgments, funding, footnotes. The second save (rusyniak_body.txt) is byte-identical to the body text of the first, so the body was read twice and completely. Both saves truncate the reference list after entry 100, so references 101 onward (the dental literature) could not be read and the total count of 113 could not be confirmed. No tables or figures in the article; the 'Author information' panel is collapsed, so the affiliation could not be checked.

design.note: narrative-review is right. The opening section is explicitly a commentary, and the whole text is a reprint, but narrative-review is the closest design in the schema and the editors' checklist applies to commentaries too.

key_findings.correction: Content confirmed; the span should be Neuropsychiatric complications ¶1-3, not ¶1-4. The 40% figure, the cited meta-analysis and the episodic-memory point are in ¶1, executive function in ¶2, fine-motor dexterity and the caudate-versus-putamen argument in ¶3. ¶4 is the anxiety, depression and psychosis paragraph, which this finding does not cover. The note is right that the 40% is cited to a study titled as concerning people with HIV.

Content confirmed; the right span is Neuropsychiatric complications ¶6-7. That section has seven paragraphs, so there is no ¶8: the symptom profile and the response to dopamine antagonists are in ¶6, and the amount-and-duration, variability and recurrence statements in ¶7.

Content confirmed; it is Neuropsychiatric complications ¶7, not ¶8. All four strands (family history, exacerbation in people with schizophrenia, unmasking, self-treatment and a shared neuronal substrate) are in that one long paragraph.

key_findings.note: Both locators right: the 1954 figure of about 2 million people in Japan and the 2008 United Nations figures (25 million amphetamines, 14 million cocaine, 11 million heroin) are in the history section ¶3, and the 200,000 with drug-induced psychosis between 1945 and 1955 in Neuropsychiatric complications ¶5.
Formication, single paragraph, all strands confirmed; the 70% is cited to the 1967 source alone, as the card's note implies. See the correction to reporting issue 2 on the substance question.

key_findings.correction: Content confirmed (26% or 40 of 150 with amphetamine addiction; 38% of 50 people addicted to cocaine; 3 hours a day on average; one person up to 14 hours; behaviour resembling the former occupation; sex differences; usually abates with abstinence; neither duration nor amount predicted it). The note is wrong on one point: the primary cocaine study is cited in the same paragraph, as reference 71 (a 2008 paper on cocaine addiction and punding by the same first author), where the review introduces punding in people who used cocaine. What is wrong is the citation at the sentence level: the 38% and the 3 hours carry reference 66 (the 2010 review) and the following sentences about 'this study' carry reference 67 (a 2009 review of dopamine dysregulation syndrome by a different group). So the figures are traceable, but not through the references attached to them.

Content confirmed; the span should be Parkinson's ¶2-3, not ¶2-4. The first three arguments (terminals rather than cell bodies, caudate rather than putamen, recovery of transporter binding after more than 12 months of abstinence) are in ¶2 and the vesicular-transporter argument in ¶3. ¶4 is the tobacco argument, which is finding 8.

Content is in Parkinson's ¶5, not ¶6 (the section has five paragraphs). Two further corrections: the review presents two studies involving the same group of patients, and the earlier age at symptom onset but not at diagnosis comes from the second of them, not from the telephone survey itself; and the interval is printed as 'confidence interval 1.6-41.4' without a level, so '95% CI' is the card's addition. Recomputed: the geometric midpoint of 1.6 and 41.4 is 8.1, consistent with the printed odds ratio of 8, and the card's caveat about its width is right.

Content confirmed (87-92% against 22%, and smoking inversely associated with Parkinson's disease, so possible partial protection); the location is Parkinson's ¶4, not ¶5. The note is right that both halves are second-hand and that the smoking proportions carry no sample, country or date.

key_findings.note: Choreoathetoid movements and dyskinesias, ¶1 for the 1974 experiment and the persistence and recurrence points, ¶2 for the treatment response, the sparse literature and the cocaine comparison. A paragraph number would make the anchor checkable.

Dental caries, single paragraph; the mechanism, the day-and-night grinding, the caries pattern and the progression to dentures all confirmed. The card is right to keep the named soft-drink brand out of the finding.

Pharmacology and toxicology ¶3-5. One clarification: the review's half-life figures are cited to its reference 22 (a 2005 literature review), not to its reference 16; the card's note could be read as saying otherwise. The cross-check against Hemphill et al. (about 10 hours, and 0.5 to 1.5 hours for cocaine) is a useful flag, and the discrepancy means neither figure should be cited from a review.

reporting_issues.note: The footnote is confirmed: the article originally appeared in the August 2011 issue of Neurologic Clinics, volume 29, number 3. The consequence (do not treat the two versions as independent sources) is right and important. The statement about how Kevil et al. (2019) cite it, including the page range, is outside this source and was not checked here.
Confirmed: the 40% sentence carries reference 26, whose title names neuropsychological impairment in people with HIV infection. The review gives no sample size or definition of 'abnormalities'.

Half of this stands and half does not. The citations are confirmed (references 43 and 46 for the 40%, reference 46 alone for the 70%), and so is the mismatch of setting: a 1969 British report and a 1967 description of amphetamine psychosis are not studies of admissions to methamphetamine treatment facilities. But 'methylamphetamine' in the 1969 title is an older name for methamphetamine, not a different substance, so the substance objection applies to the 1967 amphetamine source only. The issue should be reworded accordingly.

The sentence-level mis-citation is confirmed (references 66 and 67, both reviews, carry the figures). 'The underlying study is never cited' is wrong: it is reference 71, cited earlier in the same paragraph. The consequence should therefore be that the figures must be taken from that 2008 primary study, not that they are untraceable.

Both halves confirmed in the history section: the text attributes schedule II characterization to the Food and Drug Administration (¶2), and dates the Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act to 2005 (¶5) where Hemphill et al. date it 2006. I have no source here to say which date is right, so the card is right to send regulatory statements elsewhere.

Confirmed: the Key Points assert that dopamine receptor antagonists are the most effective treatments, while the body offers a 1974 neuroleptic study against amphetamine-induced symptoms, a 1992 hypothesis paper on formication, and a suggestion in a review that atypical antipsychotics might be tried for punding. No comparative trial anywhere in the text.
Confirmed: the commentary and Key Points address psychiatrists and psychologists, while the history section and the psychosis section address the practising neurologist.

Confirmed in substance, with one amendment: the cocaine punding figure also carries a denominator (38% of 50 patients), so the exceptions are three, not two. Everything else is as stated, including the undated smoking proportions.

The first half is confirmed (author manuscript, print citation shown as Psychiatr Clin North Am 2013;36(2):261-275 with 11 April 2013, no page numbers in the text). The second half misreads the header: the line reads 'Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2014 Jun 1', which is the PMC availability date in 2014, not an issue date of June 2013. No June 2013 date appears in the saved text. The citation year is 2013 either way.

risk_of_bias.note: Wrong instrument for the design, as on sc_hemphill_2024 and sc_matsumoto_2014: a narrative review must use the editors' narrative-review checklist with instrument 'none-applicable' (METHODS §5.3), and scripts/rob_vocab.py flags AMSTAR 2 here. Proposed checklist judgments: systematic search and explicit selection = high (none reported, single author); appraisal of the cited studies = high (only the Parkinson's telephone survey is appraised, for small size and recall bias; several frequency figures come from sources whose population or substance does not match the statement); reliance on the authors' own work = low (two self-citations out of the references I could read, both used as background); separation of evidence from speculation = high (see 'missed': the Phineas Gage passage, the inference that people seen moving abnormally in public may be showing stimulant-induced choreoathetosis, and the Key Points treatment claim are presented alongside evidence); balance = some concerns (the Parkinson's section sets the hypotheses against each other; elsewhere the framing is categorical and causal). Overall = high. The card's AMSTAR reasoning carries over in substance: useful for clinical description and for the older literature, no figure citable from it.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' is right and every element checks out: the commentary's causal framing ('slowly damaging', 'preferentially causes'), 'devastating effects' in the Summary, the Key Points treatment claim with no trial behind it, the 40% figure traced to a study of people with HIV, and the Parkinson's section as the strongest part. The card's point that the body twice raises the possibility that deficits precede use, while the commentary does not, is confirmed (Neuropsychiatric complications ¶2 and the punding section).

missed: The review states near the end of the pharmacology section that the similarities between methamphetamine, amphetamine, cocaine and MDMA make the whole discussion of neurological complications largely translatable to those drugs. That is a substance-level generalization with nothing behind it, and it matters here because this encyclopedia files claims per substance and because several of the review's own figures are in fact about amphetamine or cocaine. The card records the sentence in the exposure field but does not flag it in the interpretation gap.

Two speculative passages are not recorded: the comparison of people who use methamphetamine to 'a modern Phineas Gage' with impaired memory leaving them 'doomed to repeat' past mistakes (Neuropsychiatric complications ¶1-2), and the suggestion in the choreoathetoid section that many homeless people seen moving abnormally in city streets may be showing stimulant-induced choreoathetosis. The second is an unevidenced inference about a vulnerable group; under METHODS §9 neither should be carried into any monograph, and the card should say so.

The history section attributes the 2006 fall in treatment admissions to the precursor legislation of the preceding year, on the authority of one review, and reports manufacture costs and earnings sourced to a university web page with a 2011 access date. A policy-effect claim from a single secondary source and figures from a web page that may no longer resolve should both be flagged as uncitable, alongside the United Nations annual-report web citation behind the 25, 14 and 11 million figures.

The review's vocabulary throughout is 'abuse', 'abusers', 'addicts' and 'epidemic'. The card paraphrases in person-first language, which is right, but a note that every paraphrase from this source must be reworded (METHODS §9) would help whoever drafts from it.
other_notes: design_detail says 113 references and no tables or figures. No tables or figures is confirmed; the reference count is not checkable, because both saves cut off after entry 100 (the dental references and any beyond are missing). If the count matters for the card, it should be taken from the publisher version.

funding and declared_conflicts confirmed word for word (two United States Public Health Service grants; nothing to disclose; editorial assistance acknowledged). The affiliation in funding.affiliations_note could not be checked; the statement that the author's own research is on methamphetamine thermoregulation is consistent with two self-cited references but was not verified.
replication.timeline is consistent with the text for every entry I could check, including the 2001 transporter-recovery study linked to volkow_2001b and the 2007 meta-analysis linked to scott_2007.

The half-life discrepancy between this review and Hemphill et al. (12 versus about 10 hours; 90 versus 30 to 90 minutes for cocaine) is worth carrying as a cross-source flag on both cards, since both figures are second-hand.
